card.name: Clare Lancers Set
card.tagline: A popular Irish square set dance from County Clare featuring five distinct figures.
card.profile: The Clare Lancers Set is a prominent Irish dance performed in a square formation by four couples. Originating from the mid-west coast of Ireland, it consists of five figures danced to reels. The style emphasizes smooth, flat-footed movement.
card.insight: In the fifth figure of the Clare Lancers Set, eight dancers transition from a square formation into a column facing outward, a unique spatial shift in the Irish set dancing repertoire.
card.profile_long: The Clare Lancers Set is a cornerstone of the Irish set dancing tradition, hailing from the Clare region on the mid-west coast of the Republic of Ireland. It is recognized as one of the most popular sets within the broader Irish repertoire. The dance is structured as a square set, requiring four couples to participate. The positioning of the dancers is precise: the first top couple stands with their backs to the band, while the second top couple stands opposite them. The first side couple is positioned to the left of the first top couple when facing into the set, and the second side couple stands opposite them, to the right of the first top couple. Throughout the dance, the gentlemen remain on the left side of their partners. The aesthetic of the Clare Lancers Set is defined by its footwork. Traditionally, the figures are performed with smooth, flowing steps that push flat along the floor, characterized by a notable lack of excessive heel lift. The dance is composed of five distinct figures, all performed to the rhythm of reels. The bar counts for these figures are as follows: 160 bars for the first figure, 192 bars for the second, 144 bars for the third, 192 bars for the fourth, and 192 bars for the fifth. The fifth figure is particularly notable for its spatial transition; at the end of the chain, the couples align to form a column of eight dancers. In this formation, each lady stands in front of her partner, with the couples ordered as follows: the dancing couple, the couple on their left, the couple on their right, and the couple opposite, all facing outward from the dancing couple's original place. A specific element found in the set is the 'Big Christmas' or 'Basket' move. To execute this, a dancer places their right arm around the waist of the person to their right at the level of the small of the back, while placing their left hand over the right arm of the person to their left, clasping the right wrist of the next person. To 'Basket left,' the dancer places their right foot in the center with the knee bent slightly, hopping on this foot while pushing with the other foot placed behind. To 'Basket right,' the footwork is reversed. The dance is documented in several key texts, including Larry Lynch's 'Set Dances of Ireland,' Terry Moylan's 'Irish Dances,' Pat Murphy's 'Toss the Feathers,' and Tom Quinn's 'Irish Dancing.' While these sources provide the structural framework and specific figures, many details regarding the musical accompaniment, specific tempo, and historical origins remain undocumented in the provided materials.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originates from the Clare area on the mid-west coast of the Republic of Ireland. It is a well-documented set within the Irish dancing tradition, appearing in multiple instructional texts from the late 20th century.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in a square set of four couples. Figures are danced to reels with smooth, flat-footed steps. The fifth figure concludes with a column formation of eight dancers. The 'Basket' move involves specific arm-clasping and hopping footwork.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is performed to reels. Specific instruments are not described in sources.
sections.notable_figures: Larry Lynch, Terry Moylan, Pat Murphy, Tom Quinn, and Joe O'Hara are cited as sources for instructions or versions of the set.
sections.regional_variants: Versions of this set are available through various instructors, including Joe O'Hara and the Newcastle Irish Set Dancers.
